AI already drafts first-pass requirement documents and meeting summaries.
Business analysis gets sold two contradictory ways online.

blocks.heading: Real Skill Test Before Anything Else

items.text: Most "is business analyst a good career" articles start with salary.
A requirement almost never arrives clean.
The business analyst's actual job is not writing down what was said.

blocks.heading: Why "Business Analyst" Is Not One Job

items.text: This is the part most generic BA content flattens into one job description.
These four tracks are ordered by real growth headroom, not by how common the entry point is or which one is talked about most.
Banking, insurance, and healthcare follow because domain trust compounds pay quickly inside a regulated sector.

blocks.heading: Questions Before You Commit to This Path

items.text: A salary chart or one relative's opinion about "business analyst scope" cannot tell you whether this fits your specific situation.
Do you feel more energised sitting in a room where three people describe the same problem three different ways, or does that scenario sound exhausting before it even starts.
Can your situation absorb an MBA fee and two lost earning years for a faster, higher-paying entry, or does a lower-cost, slower-building non-MBA route fit your runway better.

blocks.heading: Avoid When Deciding on Business Analysis

items.text: "Not coding" is not the same as "easier." The real skill bar here is precision under ambiguity, extracting a clear, buildable requirement from a room of disagreeing stakeholders, which most people are genuinely bad at by default and cannot fake for long.
An MBA can genuinely speed up entry at consulting firms and large enterprises.
IT-services BA work rotates you across client accounts fast, which builds breadth early.

blocks.heading: MBA Vs No-MBA Entry Routes
rows: Speed to first offer
Fastest for campus-hire consulting and large-enterprise BA programmes, placement cells route MBA graduates directly into structured BA or associate-consultant tracks.
Slower on average, because there is no campus pipeline doing the sourcing for you, but IT services and banking hire "any graduate" year-round once you have a proof-of-work artifact.
Upfront cost
High. A two-year full-time MBA at a brand-name institute can cost several lakh rupees before you earn a single BA rupee, plus the opportunity cost of two years out of the workforce.
Low. A business requirement document, a process map, and an ECBA certificate together cost a fraction of one MBA semester.
Starting pay ceiling
Higher on day one, especially at consulting firms and large enterprises that run dedicated MBA-entry BA or associate-consultant bands.
Lower on day one, but the gap narrows fast once you have 2-3 years of real requirement-ownership and domain depth behind you.
What actually closes the gap later
The MBA brand opens the door faster; it does not automatically make you better at extracting a clear requirement from a confused stakeholder, that is still a built skill, not a taught one.
Domain depth, a track record of projects that shipped on scope, and (later) CBAP close most of the pay gap by the 4-6 year mark, without the MBA fee or the two lost years.

blocks.heading: Real BA Salary Bands
rows: IT services / consulting BA, fresher
Rs 3.5-6 LPA
The widest and most crowded entry door. Pay depends heavily on the specific IT-services firm and whether you enter with any proof artifact beyond a degree.
MBA-entry BA / associate consultant, fresher
Rs 6-12 LPA
Consulting firms and large enterprises running campus BA hiring pay meaningfully more from day one, but weigh this against the MBA fee and two lost earning years before treating it as a clean win.
Banking / BFSI BA, fresher to 2 years
Rs 5-9 LPA
Structured graduate and management-trainee BA programmes at banks and large NBFCs often out-pay generalist IT-services BA roles once domain training completes.
Any track, 3-6 years, real requirement ownership
Rs 8-15 LPA
The single biggest lever at this stage is not years of experience. It is whether you own requirements end to end or still hand off the hard decisions to a senior BA.
Senior or lead BA, 6-10 years
Rs 15-25 LPA
CBAP-certified professionals and BAs with deep domain trust in one regulated sector (banking, insurance, healthcare) commonly sit at the top of this band.
BA moved into product management, 7+ years total
Rs 20-35 LPA and above

This is the track where the numbers stop looking like a BA salary at all. The step happens because the work changes, you start owning outcomes, not just documenting them, not because the job title alone commands more money.

blocks.heading: Business Analyst Career Path
rows: Associate or junior BA
Fresher to about 2 years
You write what a senior asked for. You own notes, process maps and clean documents, not the scope call.
ECBA, which IIBA describes as the first step for people starting out. Its page states no experience requirement.
Business analyst
About 3 to 6 years
You own requirements for one feature or process end to end and defend them to stakeholders.
CCBA. IIBA lists two to three years of work experience in the last seven years (3,750 hours).
Senior BA
About 6 to 10 years
You choose what is worth building, rank the work, and say no to scope. Juniors and BAs hand their hard calls to you.
CBAP. IIBA lists five or more years of work experience in the last 10 years (7,500 hours).
Lead BA or BA manager
Often 8 to 12 years, varies by employer
You own a team's output, staffing and quality across projects, and you advise the sponsor, not only document for them.
CBAP still fits. IIBA's roadmap names BA project lead, program lead, practice lead and BA manager. No credential is required for the manager step.
Head of BA or centre of excellence
Usually 12 or more, employer-specific
You set the method, hiring and standards for a whole function and answer for results to senior leaders.
None defines this step. IIBA does not name a head-of-BA title, so judge it by domain depth, proof and leadership record.

blocks.heading: Who Should Not Choose Business Analysis
rows: You want a fixed, well-defined task list every morning

Requirements shift, scope gets renegotiated mid-project, and a sponsor can change direction after weeks of work. If ambiguity genuinely drains you rather than sharpens you, this role will feel exhausting no matter how good the pay looks.
You are choosing an MBA mainly to "become a BA" without checking fit first
An MBA opens doors faster, but it will not make stakeholder-extraction skill appear on its own. Test the ambiguity-tolerance question below before spending on the degree, not after.
You want to avoid sitting through disagreement between people who outrank you

A meaningful share of the job is standing in a room while a sponsor and a delivery lead disagree about scope, and being the person who has to write down the version everyone can actually live with. That pressure does not go away with seniority, it usually gets heavier.
You assume "business analyst" and "product manager" are basically the same job

They overlap, but a BA who has only ever documented requirements handed down from someone else has not yet built the ownership and trade-off judgement a PM role tests for. That gap needs deliberate closing, not an assumption that the title alone transfers.

visuals.heading: Will AI Replace Business Analysts

items.text: First-draft business requirement documents from a recorded stakeholder meeting, using transcription and summarisation tools now built into Confluence, Notion, and dedicated meeting-notes apps.
Turning a rough requirement into a first-pass set of user stories with draft acceptance criteria, cutting the blank-page time on routine, well-understood requests.
Generating a first current-state process map from a described workflow, which used to be a slow manual diagramming task.

blocks.heading: Not a Flat Yes or No

items.text: You get real energy from resolving disagreement and structuring an ambiguous problem, not just documenting a clear one.
You have honestly weighed the MBA-vs-no-MBA cost and speed trade-off against your own runway, not just picked the option that sounds more prestigious.
You are willing to build domain depth in one sector (banking, insurance, healthcare, or IT-services breadth) rather than treating "business analyst" as one interchangeable generic title.
You are open to the BA-to-product-manager bridge later, on purpose, rather than assuming the title alone will carry you there.
